zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check, consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, page subset supplied in this package; CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . This is a lexical aid, not authority for this copy’s glyphs or layout.

lines.note: Mawari here means any dish other than rice. The first line is a flush-left headword, not an indented continuation; the narrow word space in Qualquer iguaria is visible.

runs.text: ura q̃ comummente vsão as molheres ajuntan-

lines.note: Completes palaura and explains that women commonly use this expression with a prefix added. Preserve the unexpanded q̃ and the historical spelling vsão.
Completes ajuntando-lhe: the added prefix is Von. In the example the mark over o in Võmauariga is a tilde, unlike the distinct caron in nǒte; the worn following m is not an extra i.
Completes meiwaku ja: lack of accompanying dishes causes trouble or distress. The Portuguese begins 'having no various dishes, I have ...', with the feeling expressed below.
Pena completes the statement of distress at lacking dishes. The row closes the food-related Mawari, before a homonymous noun follows.
This separately printed, genuinely indented Mawari means a circuit or going around. Its indentation is preserved even though it is a headword.
The verb mawari means going around or circling. Preserve its abbreviated u and atta principal parts and the Portuguese alternatives.
Shiro no ushiro e mawaru means going around to the back of a fortress. The Portuguese verb rodear continues with that location on the next row.
Completes rodear a fortaleza por de tras, going around behind the fortress. The printed de tras remains two words.
Mawarimeguri combines going around with making a circuit; rodear supplies the concise Portuguese equivalent. The two t types in utta are retained.

runs.text: Fazer bailar, ou cãtar os Mais.

lines.note: Mawase here concerns causing the mai performances to be danced or sung. Mais is the Japanese performance term pluralized within the Portuguese explanation, not the ordinary Portuguese adverb mais.

The headword is Mauaxi, not OCR Manaxi: mawasu makes something go around. The principal part aita records the historical mawaita inflection, not modern mawashita; the supplied historical-language notes discuss this very entry.
Completes andar à roda, then gives kaibun wo mawasu, circulating a written message. Man- begins mandar, explained over the following rows.

runs.text: dar hum meſmo recado, ou carta a muitas

lines.note: Completes mandar: sending the same message or letter to many destinations. This is circulation of one communication, not several unrelated letters.
Completes the circular-message example and introduces tsukai wo mawasu, sending a messenger around. The translation continues with the messenger and destinations below.

runs.text: algum homem com recado a varias partes,

lines.note: The messenger is a person sent with a communication to various places. Preserve the uncontracted algum here, without importing a tilde from other entries.
Adds 'or locations', closing the explanation of sending a messenger around. It is a short continuation rather than a separate sense of the next headword.
Maō is explained as the king of tengu and rendered 'king of devils'. This preserves the dictionary's religious equivalence; the marked vowels remain carons as printed.
Maotoko denotes a man in an adulterous relationship. The Portuguese specifies a woman whose married status is stated on the next row.
Casada completes 'married woman'. Maotoko wo suru is then illustrated from the woman's perspective as having another man besides her husband.

runs.text: a molher com outro ſegundo a fora o ſeu pro-

lines.note: Continues the description of the woman being with another, additional man outside her own marriage. Preserve the source's a fora spacing and the divided pro-.
Completes proprio marido, 'her own husband'. This closes the adultery example before the unrelated fence entry.

runs.text: Sebeſinha, ou cerca de caninhas que ſe

lines.note: Maxe is a small hedge or fence of thin canes. The damaged final headword letter has the form of e, supported by the following Maxegaqi; OCR Maxo would obscure the connection.

runs.text: faz a o redor dalgũa roſeira, ou eruas que dão

lines.note: The fence is made around a rosebush or other productive plants. The separated a o and the tilde over u in dalgũa are retained as printed.

Completes the definition of Maxe: a little enclosure around plants that bear flowers. The scan clearly reads fulas, not flores; retain this historical word. Lexical comparator, consulted after reading: Macau Cultural Affairs Bureau, “Portuguese Lexicon,” entry fula/fulas, https://www.icm.gov.mo/rc/viewer/20033/1289. The complete short line and adjacent rule are inside the crop.

Maxegaqi names the same kind of small fence as Maxe; the Portuguese Idem explicitly refers back. Preserve the q and the roman headword against italic Idem; the worn central letters do not justify changing the spelling.
Mano iqiuoi explains Maxei as the demon's force or fury, matching the Portuguese. Read iqiuoi with q, not a modernized ki spelling; all Japanese words are roman and the Portuguese gloss is italic.

This noun means a monkey: the printer recommends Maxira, followed by Portuguese Bugio. Preserve the visible italic setting of the preferred form as well as the Latin label, rather than mechanically making all Japanese-looking words roman; retain the candidate's accent where the small mark remains compatible.

The verb means to exceed or surpass. The historical ſu/aita principal parts are retained; the Portuguese reads the single word ſobrepojar, not the OCR split ſobre pojar. Bu- begins the example continued on the next row, and its hyphen is retained.

Joins the preceding Bu- to form Buguen and says that wealth or standing increases exceptionally. The Portuguese explanation begins “to be much more”; retain the printed cotonofoca and maſu rather than introducing modern word boundaries or s.

Completes the Portuguese interpretation as richer and more powerful than before. Sonata- begins a new Japanese example and is visibly roman after the paragraph mark; preserve the physical line break within Sonatano.

Completes Sonatano toxiga maxita, comparing the addressee's age with the speaker's. The scan supports maxita with x and the Portuguese says the addressee is older; retain the terminal comma for the continuation below.
Ends the age comparison with “older than I.” Corega maxi- begins the next Japanese example about one thing being better; preserve the paragraph division, roman example, and final hyphen.

runs.text: l, potiùs, Maxita. Iſto he milhor. ¶

lines.note: Completes Corega maxigia and gives the preferred wording Maxita, interpreted as “this is better.” The preferred form is visibly italic with the surrounding editorial words; preserve that setting, historical milhor, and the To- that continues below.

The preceding To- completes Toximaxi, followed by the alternative toximaſari, both meaning older in age. Correct the OCR's fused ximaxial to ximaxi. l, with the visible full stop and the alternative marker distinguished; do not add a phantom a before l.
The noun denotes excess or advantage, consistent with the preceding verb “surpass.” Retain the printed historical ventagem and the long-s sequence in Exceſſo; this is a separate flush-left headword.

Maxiba is identified with Xiba, cut branches or brushwood. The P. label is set upright in this line and is returned to roman; the Japanese synonym remains roman and the Portuguese definition begins at Ramos, continuing below.

Finishes the definition with cut branches of trees or plants. Keep cortados as printed, agreeing with the earlier Ramos, rather than changing it to match the adjacent plantas; the short indented continuation is complete in the crop.

runs.text: Paßarinho aßi chamado, que cãta bẽ.

lines.note: Maxico names a small bird said to sing well. Preserve the two distinct nasal abbreviations cãta and bẽ and both ß forms; the Portuguese makes the referent clear without licensing a modern species name in the transcription.

The honorific verb is glossed with several Portuguese verbs of existence, state, and coming. The scan supports Maximaxi and ſu/xita; retain Auer and the comma because the list and usage restriction continue below.

runs.text: ter, &c. Vſaſe falando de Deos, dos ſan-

lines.note: Continues the honorific verb's meanings with “have” and restricts its use to God, saints, and noble persons. Preserve Vſaſe and the san-/ctos division. This continuation is visibly inset from the headword margin, so its missing indentation is restored.

Completes ſan-ctos and the reference to noble persons. The ct is closely set but both letters belong to the word; retain the two long s letters in peſſoas and the final S. label. Restore the observed continuation indentation.

Maxira is glossed by Saru and Portuguese Bugio, confirming “monkey.” Preserve the locally sloping P. label as italic, with its full stop, and keep the Japanese synonym upright; no linguistic expansion of P. is inserted into the text.

The expression means “how much more” or “all the more.” The x and the terminal ya are legible, and the concise italic Portuguese gloss matches the Japanese expression without any missing continuation.
Extends the preceding expression with iuan, “how much more shall we say.” The scan has iuan, not a normalized iwan; retain the comma and &c. of the Portuguese gloss.

The paired noun describes superiority and inferiority, literally surpassing and being surpassed. Preserve the headword's visible word division Maxi votori, distinct from the compounded example below, and the final Portuguese hyphen.

Completes ſobrepoja-do and begins the example that neither has an advantage or disadvantage. The Portuguese Não continues at the top of column 2. Restore the visible indentation while preserving the column break and unjoined Japanese spelling.

runs.text: auia em nenhum delles exceſſo, nem ſer in

lines.note: Continues Não from column 1: neither was superior or inferior. The scan ends this row with bare in, without a secure hyphen; retain that physical division rather than silently completing inferior here. The native crop includes the full row and right rule.

Completes in-ferior from the preceding physical row and closes the comparison of equals. No text is missing between the two rows; preserve the short italic fragment and full stop without inventing a hyphen above.

Tenmano ſauari explains obstruction by a demon, matching the Portuguese impediment. The caron over ǒ is visible and must not be flattened or changed to a circumflex. Restore the flush-left headword placement; the baseline incorrectly treated it as a continuation.

The example enjoins the reader not to be hindered by demonic interference. Retain the historical passive ſayeraruru and the caron in Maxǒni; the negative Portuguese translation continues on the next row.

Completes the Portuguese admonition not to be impeded and tempted by the devil. The initial long s, the conjunction, and the final full stop are supported by the scan; this remains an indented continuation.

This entry is the demon's place, as Tenmano tocoro and Lugar do diabo agree. Correct OCR Tenmnano to Tenmano: the broken strokes belong to one m, not mn. Preserve the unaccented o in Maxo and restore the flush-left headword placement.

Describes an honest, straightforward person, distinct from the demonic homophones above. The small caron is visible; preserve Peßoa, long s in ſimples, and the printed recta. Restore the headword's flush-left alignment.

Suyeno yaxiro explains a subsidiary shrine; the Portuguese calls it a shrine of the Camis. Camis is a Japanese term embedded in the italic explanation and is flagged for whole-word typeface review. Restore flush-left placement of this new entry.

runs.text: que he inferior, & ſubordenada a outra prin-

lines.note: Continues the subsidiary-shrine definition: it is subordinate to another principal shrine. The worn letter after b is o, while enlargement shows e, not i, after d: retain the printed ſubordenada without modernizing it. Preserve the terminal prin- and the original spelling he.

The left fragment completes prin-cipal from the Maxxa definition. At the far right of this same physical row, the scan prints a parenthesis-like mark and idades., semantically completing the following Maxxe definition. Merge the duplicate provisional c2-l011 into this row, retain the mark and displaced word at the far right, and do not relocate them into logical reading order. The crop contains both fragments, their full glyphs, and the right rule.

Suyeno yo explains the last or latter ages. The scan reads Vltimos with a narrow l after V, omitted by the OCR. Its terminal “or ages” is physically displaced to the preceding row and retained there; no text is added to this line to regularize the layout.

The verb means to reduce something to powder. A renewed native enlargement after the NINJAL lexical check confirms two joined long s letters: correct ſuru to ſſuru, retaining the printed unusual principal part rather than regularizing it. Preserve the tilde over u in algũa and the final em, whose complement begins below.

Completes the definition “to powder or grind” and gives an example about grinding medicine. Preserve the historical Portuguese poo, the single long s in Cuſuriuo, and the doubled long s in maſſuru; the language change after Vt, is visible.

The Portuguese interprets the medicine example as grinding or breaking down medicines. Chauo then starts a separate Japanese example about tea; it is roman and continues below rather than belonging to the preceding Portuguese sentence.
Completes Chauo maſſuru, “grind tea.” Preserve the doubled long s and the printed italic Cha; this embedded term is flagged for human whole-word typeface inspection rather than silently resetting it.
The adjective denotes something very white. The doubled x and final roi are visible and accord with the intensive sense; retain the roman headword and italic Portuguese gloss with its long s.
This adjectival form has the same “very white” meaning as Maxxiroi. The na ending and Idem are legible; preserve the change of ending rather than treating this as a duplicate row.

Names great honesty or candour. The g after ǒ is worn but its lower loop remains, and the adjacent adjectival entry supports the reading; retain the caron, giqi spelling, and the printed Portuguese candura.

The adjectival counterpart means very straightforward or honest. Preserve the distinct giqina ending and visible caron; the Portuguese ſimples here has the favourable sense established by candura above.

runs.text: Diante, ou em preſença, ou dantes.

lines.note: Maye receives both spatial “in front/in one's presence” and temporal “before” senses. Preserve the historical ye spelling and the Portuguese preſença with cedilla; the row starts a new flush-left entry.

The example means before someone comes; Japanese Mairanu maye is compatible with Portuguese Antes que venha. Retain the paragraph sign, the unjoined words, and the italic gloss, with no modernization of the negative form.

This example concerns someone's turn or allotted responsibility. Restore the clearly printed paragraph sign omitted by the OCR; Sonatano mayede gozaru is roman, while the Portuguese ends with the divided voſ-.

Completes voſ-ſa and explains “your turn” or “belongs to you.” Correct the damaged OCR vnas to the scan's vos and Mieca to Micca, supported by the visible double c and the following translation “three days.” Preserve the printed separation pertence vos and the divided ma-.

Completes Micca mayeni and states that the action was performed three days earlier. The scan supports both cedillas in tçucamatçutte and the damaged but readable gozaru; the Portuguese begins Ha and continues below.
Completes “I did that three days ago,” then starts an example about conformity to reason. The visible caron belongs to ǒ in dǒrino; keep the worn following letters as rino and preserve the ß in ißo.

The Portuguese says that this accords with reason. Although mayede would fit the entry and expression, the first printed letter looks like n, and the existing nayede is retained as a nonblocking scan-level caveat rather than silently corrected from Japanese expectations.
Finishes the alternate Portuguese interpretation as clear or evident reason. Retain rezão, its tilde over a, and the long italic line continuation; the short row is fully present in the crop.

runs.text: Maye. Aſano coromo. i, Nunono coromo.

lines.note: This homograph denotes a hemp or cloth garment, explained by Aſano coromo and Nunono coromo. Both Japanese synonym phrases are roman; preserve the long s in Aſano and the punctuation around i, without flagging these standalone synonyms as embedded terms.

The Portuguese defines a hemp garment, followed by an example combining rough clothing with sitting on grass. Correct the candidate's sôza- to sǒza- because the native mark is a caron. Preserve canemo and the line-end hyphen.

Completes Maye sǒzani xite curaſu and begins its explanation as living in coarse clothing. Join the OCR's veſtid o to veſtido. Read the worn final word as großeiro rather than großeno: the narrow i/r junction is compatible with that lexical reading but remains a nonblocking caveat; preserve the visible ß rather than expanding it.

Finishes the austere-living example with staying upon the grass. Preserve the two long-s forms, historical eruas, and the final S. label; the physical line and its continuation indentation remain separate from the next headword.

Mayeaxi denotes an animal's front feet, with Atoaxi introducing the rear feet explained below. The scan has a semicolon after animal, not the provisional comma; retain Pès and the upright contrasting Japanese word.

Provides the Portuguese meaning of Atoaxi from the previous row: the rear feet. Preserve traſeiros with long s and the separate indented row; there is no additional Japanese headword hidden in this short continuation.

runs.text: Serra com que ſe ſerra algum pao

lines.note: The entry names a saw used for sawing a piece of wood lengthwise. The q in biqi is visible; preserve the Portuguese distinction between capital Serra and the verb ſerra, and do not add a tilde to the printed pao.
Completes the saw definition with “lengthwise.” Both words and the full stop are clear; retain the continuation indentation and do not combine the physical row with the previous one.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de auental de caſca

lines.note: Mayecaqe is an apron, here a kind made from bark. Retain the tilde on u in Hũa, the historical auental, and the q in the Japanese headword; the material description continues on the next row.

runs.text: de aruore que cingem os caçadores por diante,

lines.note: Specifies tree bark and that hunters gird the apron in front. The scan supports the cedilla in caçadores and the final comma; retain aruore rather than modernizing its consonants.

runs.text: ou outra gente que anda nos matos.

lines.note: Extends the use of the bark apron to other people who go through the woods. Preserve the printed wording and terminal full stop; the row is not a new entry despite its self-contained clause.
Mayeda is identified with Cadota, a field before or near the house. Preserve both Japanese forms in roman and the historical Varzea; dian- remains physically divided from te below.

runs.text: te da caſa, ou perto da caſa.

lines.note: Completes dian-te and explains the field's location before or near the house. Both instances of caſa contain long s. Restore the visibly inset continuation indentation omitted by the provisional Markdown.

runs.text: Cana do arco da banda de dentro,

lines.note: Mayedaqe names the bamboo on the inner side of a bow. Preserve the headword's q and the Portuguese material term Cana; the comma leads into a fuller explanation on the following physical row.

runs.text: ou bambu que eſta arcado da parte de dentro do

lines.note: Further describes the bamboo curved on the inside of the bow. Retain the unaccented eſta and printed arcado rather than modernizing them; restore the continuation's visible indentation.

Completes the inner-bow definition, then contrasts Todaqe, the outer bamboo. The separate roman word is followed by its own italic gloss. Preserve fo- and restore indentation; do not promote the inline contrast to a new physical headword row.
Completes fo-ra do arco, identifying the outer side of the bow. Preserve the short separate row and full stop, and restore the inset continuation placement seen in the scan.

The noun is an apron; Mayedareuo begins an example of putting one on. The scan supports the printed historical Auental and the roman Japanese example following the paragraph mark; no line-end hyphen is present.
Completes Mayedareuo ſuru and glosses putting on or girding an apron. Preserve the initial long s and the printed unaccented Por; restore the indentation of this continuation.

runs.text: Certa taboa que ha no carro, em que

lines.note: Mayeita names a particular board on a carriage used by noble people. Retain taboa and the small but visible no, whose o is weak; the relative clause continues to the final body row.

Completes the carriage-board explanation with noble people mounting it. Restore continuation indentation and retain the initial long s and ß in peßoas. Maye. at the far right is a catchword, not part of this sentence; it is restored in a separate furniture zone, while the body crop intentionally retains that right-edge context.
